title: Story vs Discourse
description: Genette's distinction — what's told and how it's told

concepts.title: The Basic Distinction
concepts.contentHtml:
Narrative theory's foundational distinction: between the story (what happens) and the discourse (how it's told). Same story can be told many ways.

French structuralists called these histoire and récit. Genette added a third term, narration. Russian Formalists used fabula (story material) and syuzhet (plot as constructed).

The distinction lets analysis attend separately to the events themselves and to the techniques by which events are presented to a reader.

concepts.title: Genette
concepts.contentHtml:
Gérard Genette's Narrative Discourse (1972, English 1980) is the central work of modern narrative theory. Built around close analysis of Proust's In Search of Lost Time.

Three main axes: tense (relations between time of story and time of narration — order, duration, frequency), mood (focalisation), and voice (who narrates).

The book's vocabulary — diegesis, focalisation, analepsis, prolepsis — has become standard.

concepts.title: Diegesis and Mimesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Two ancient terms revived by narrative theory.

Diegesis: telling. The narrator reports events.

Mimesis: showing. Events are dramatised, often through dialogue, as if the reader witnesses them directly.

The distinction goes back to Plato (Republic, Book 3). Genette uses 'diegetic' more broadly: the world of the story. Extradiegetic = outside the story. Intradiegetic = inside it.

concepts.title: What Story-Discourse Lets Us See
concepts.contentHtml:
The distinction makes formal choices visible. Why does a novel begin where it does? Why this point of view rather than another? Why this temporal arrangement?

Two novels with identical stories — same events, same characters — can be radically different works because of discourse choices. Lolita told from Dolores's perspective is a different book.

Recognising story-discourse separately also clarifies adaptation. Films of novels keep most of the story but transform the discourse.

concepts.title: Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
The story-discourse distinction is heuristic, not absolute. In some narratives the line blurs: heavily metafictional works (Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler), works where the discourse is itself the story (Beckett's late prose).

Some critics (Jonathan Culler, others) have argued that 'story' is itself reconstructed by readers from the discourse — there's no story prior to the telling.

The distinction remains useful as a tool, with awareness of its limits.

title: Time in Narrative
description: Order, duration, frequency — temporal play in fiction

concepts.title: Order
concepts.contentHtml:
Genette's first temporal category: order. Story events happen in some chronological order; discourse may present them in a different order.

Analepsis (flashback): discourse goes back in time to an earlier event.

Prolepsis (flashforward): discourse jumps ahead. 'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember...' (García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude opening).

Modern fiction routinely deploys complex order. Faulkner, Pynchon, Kate Atkinson's Life After Life.

concepts.title: Duration
concepts.contentHtml:
The relationship between time of story and time of discourse — pages per event.

Scene: discourse time roughly matches story time. Dialogue mostly works this way.

Summary: discourse compresses story. 'Three years passed.'

Ellipsis: discourse skips story time entirely.

Pause: discourse continues while story stops. Description, narrator's commentary.

Stretch: discourse expands story. A second of consciousness across pages (Joyce's Bloom on Sandymount Strand).

concepts.title: Frequency
concepts.contentHtml:
How often discourse tells what happened how often in story.

Singulative: telling once what happened once. Standard.

Repetitive: telling several times what happened once. Multiple narrators on the same event (The Sound and the Fury; Rashomon).

Iterative: telling once what happened several times. 'Every Sunday she went to mass.'

Proust's iteratives are famous — the elaborate description of a single sample of a habitual act.

concepts.title: Anachrony
concepts.contentHtml:
Anachrony: any departure of discourse from chronological order.

Genette analysed Proust's Recherche in detail. Some anachronies are internal (within the story's main timeframe) and some external (reaching outside it).

The technical apparatus matters less than the underlying point: temporal play in narrative is one of fiction's main resources, and modern fiction has developed it intensively.

concepts.title: Why It Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Time in narrative isn't just style. It's how meaning accumulates.

A novel that announces the protagonist's death in its first line and then circles back through the day that led to it (García Márquez's Chronicle of a Death Foretold) builds different meanings than chronological narration would. The reader knows the future while watching the past.

The basic discovery of 20th-century narrative: time can be one of the novelist's primary instruments. Naïve chronological telling is one option among many.

title: Focalization & Point of View
description: Who sees, who speaks — the seeing instance

concepts.title: Genette's Innovation
concepts.contentHtml:
Pre-Genette criticism used 'point of view' to talk about both who narrates and whose perspective the events are filtered through. Genette separated these.

Voice: who speaks (narrates). Focalisation: who sees.

Often these coincide. A first-person narrator typically speaks and sees. But not always. A first-person narrator can report what another character saw. A third-person narrator can present events from inside a particular character's consciousness.

concepts.title: Types of Focalisation
concepts.contentHtml:
Zero focalisation (omniscient): the narrator knows everything. 19th-century novels often use this.

Internal focalisation: events are presented through one character's perspective.

External focalisation: events are presented from outside any character's consciousness. Hemingway's later style approaches this.

Internal focalisation can be fixed (one character throughout), variable (different characters in different sections), or multiple (the same event from multiple perspectives).

concepts.title: First, Second, Third Person
concepts.contentHtml:
Voice's main grammatical option.

First person: 'I.' The narrator is a character in the story. Range from full reliability to extreme unreliability.

Third person: 'he/she.' The narrator is outside the story. Can be omniscient or limited.

Second person: 'you.' Rare and difficult to sustain. Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler; Bright Lights, Big City; parts of Bolaño.

Most novels use first or third.

concepts.title: Free Indirect Discourse
concepts.contentHtml:
The most flexible technique for representing minds in third-person narrative: free indirect discourse.

The narrator's third-person voice is inflected by a character's thought without quotation marks or explicit attribution. 'No — she shouldn't be here at all.' Whose voice? Both at once.

Pioneered by Austen, perfected by Flaubert, central to Joyce and Woolf.

concepts.title: Why Choice Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Each focalisation choice creates different reader experience.

Omniscient narration creates a sense of moral framework — a knower above the action. Internal focalisation creates intimacy with one consciousness. External focalisation creates distance and ambiguity.

The choice also constrains plot. A first-person narrator can't report scenes they weren't present at without contortion. An internally-focalised narrative can't reveal what the focal character doesn't know.

title: Free Indirect Discourse
description: Voice that hovers between narrator and character

concepts.title: What FID Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Free indirect discourse (FID) blends a narrator's voice with a character's. It uses the third person and past tense of standard narration but the vocabulary, syntax, and emotional register of the character whose mind we're in.

Direct: She thought, 'I shouldn't be here.'

Indirect: She thought that she shouldn't be there.

Free indirect: No — she shouldn't be here at all.

The third version sounds like the character but is delivered by the narrator. The reader hears both at once.

concepts.title: Austen and the Beginning
concepts.contentHtml:
Jane Austen is generally credited with the first sustained use of FID in English fiction. Emma (1815) is the canonical example.

Emma Woodhouse's misperceptions about people are filtered through her own consciousness, in language hovering between her perspective and the narrator's. The reader sees what Emma sees while also seeing how Emma is wrong.

The technique is what makes Austen's irony possible. The narrator never says 'Emma was being foolish.' The text shows Emma being foolish in her own voice.

concepts.title: Flaubert
concepts.contentHtml:
Flaubert perfected FID in French. Madame Bovary (1856) sustains it for hundreds of pages — Emma's romantic delusions filtered through her own grandiose vocabulary.

French structuralists made Flaubert central to their analysis precisely because of this technique. He demonstrated that narrative voice could be a continuous interplay rather than a fixed position.

concepts.title: Joyce and Modernist FID
concepts.contentHtml:
Modernist fiction radicalised FID. Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) opens in baby talk because the focal character is an infant: 'Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road.'

The prose evolves with Stephen's consciousness through the book. By chapter five, the language is theological abstraction.

Woolf in Mrs Dalloway shifts FID seamlessly between characters' minds within a single page. The narrator becomes a mobile presence.

concepts.title: FID Today
concepts.contentHtml:
FID is now standard equipment for serious fiction. Most contemporary literary novels use it routinely.

It allows a writer to: get inside characters without losing third-person discipline; produce irony at a character's expense without the narrator stepping forward; shift perspective fluidly; create intimate unreliability.

Without it, most of the great fiction of the past two centuries would be impossible.

title: Unreliable Narration
description: Booth's category and what it does to readers

concepts.title: The Term
concepts.contentHtml:
Wayne C. Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) introduced the term unreliable narrator: a narrator whose account the reader has reason to distrust.

Booth's working definition: a narrator is unreliable when their account diverges from the work's implied norms. The reader perceives a gap between what the narrator says and what the implied author seems to mean.

The mechanism requires the reader to do interpretive work — to register the gap and read against the narrator.

concepts.title: Types of Unreliability
concepts.contentHtml:
Narrators can be unreliable in different ways.

Factually unreliable: they get events wrong, lie, or misremember. Humbert Humbert in Lolita.

Morally unreliable: their values diverge from the work's.

Naively unreliable: they don't fully understand what they're reporting.

Mentally unreliable: their perception is impaired. The narrator of Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury's first section.

Often these combine. Pip in Great Expectations is naively unreliable as a young man and morally clearer as an older retrospective narrator.

concepts.title: How Unreliability Is Signalled
concepts.contentHtml:
The reader has to be able to detect unreliability.

Internal contradictions: the narrator says one thing then another.

External evidence: other characters' reactions, external facts.

Language choices: a narrator's vocabulary may betray attitudes they're trying to hide. Humbert's elaborate aesthetic prose around what is, plainly, child rape.

Genre and convention: readers come with expectations about reliability.

concepts.title: Major Examples
concepts.contentHtml:
Famous unreliable narrators:

Humbert Humbert, Lolita (Nabokov, 1955).

Stevens, The Remains of the Day (Ishiguro, 1989).

Patrick Bateman, American Psycho (Ellis, 1991).

Charles Kinbote, Pale Fire (Nabokov, 1962).

Amy Dunne, Gone Girl (Flynn, 2012).

Each works differently. The category is broad enough to cover most cases where the reader's interpretive work is part of the experience.

concepts.title: Why Use It
concepts.contentHtml:
Unreliable narration does things reliable narration can't.

It builds intimacy with a perspective the reader rejects. We get inside Humbert in a way that pure third-person condemnation wouldn't allow.

It makes the reader active. The text's meaning isn't fully delivered; the reader has to construct it through skepticism.

It dramatises self-deception, partial vision, the limits of any single viewpoint.

Most major modernist and postmodernist novels involve some form of unreliability.
